latest_final:
The father is himself the hostage. He has been kidnapped and is still being held captive, and the call is happening on his own smartphone in his presence, so he can hear everything. On the line is his daughter, an adult who knows the hostage personally—it is her father—and she is begging the kidnapper to spare his life. The kidnapper then shouts the demand: 100 million yen, brought alone by noon tomorrow, with no police, or the hostage dies. He is deliberately making the father listen while threatening him, using the father as leverage against the daughter.

Overhearing this, the father understands what his daughter is preparing to do: raise the 100 million yen herself and bring it alone to the kidnapper. He knows the "alone" condition would leave her unprotected, and that after she handed over the money she would be killed as a witness. So compliance would not save him; it would only put his daughter in lethal danger and enrich the kidnapper.

That is why the father decides the ransom should not be paid. His refusal is a signal and a sabotage aimed at stopping the daughter from delivering the money—his only available way, as a captive, to keep her out of the trap. He is not acting out of any belief that his own life is already lost, and he does not refuse out of principle, poverty, or because he wants the kidnapper caught. His motive is to protect his daughter: better that he remain a hostage, with rescue still possible, than that she walk alone into a delivery that would get her killed. The puzzle's twist is that the "hostage" whose life the daughter begs to spare is the very man deciding not to pay—and his decision is meant to save her, not himself.
